name: Linkage Disequilibrium Calculator
seoDesc: Linkage disequilibrium measures whether two alleles are inherited together more often than chance. Free linkage disequilibrium calculator: enter your values a
summary:
Linkage disequilibrium measures whether two alleles are inherited together more often than chance. It returns expected AB if independent, D (coefficient of disequilibrium), D′ (normalised) and r², and the panel shows all of them at once.

From the frequency of the four haplotypes you get D, the normalised D′ and r² — the number that decides whether a genetic marker can stand in for the causal variant next to it. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Linkage Disequilibrium
sections.html:
D = f(AB) − p_A·p_B. D′ = D ÷ D_max. r² = D² ÷ [p_A(1−p_A)·p_B(1−p_B)]

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Ddeviation of the observed haplotype frequency from independence—
D′D scaled to its maximum, −1 to 1—
r²the squared correlation between the two loci—

sections.title: How do I use the Linkage Disequilibrium?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the frequency of each allele and the observed frequency of the AB haplotype.
  2. D, D′ and r² are calculated together with the independent expectation.
  3. Use r² to judge whether one locus is a usable proxy for the other.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: frequency of allele a of 0.4, frequency of allele b of 0.3, frequency of haplotype ab of 0.25.

Substituting them into the formula gives expected ab if independent of 0.12, d (coefficient of disequilibrium) of 0.13, d′ (normalised) of 0.7222, r² of 0.3353.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
r² above 0.8Strong LDone locus predicts the other; a tag SNP will do
r² 0.3 – 0.8Moderatesome information is shared
r² below 0.3Weakthe loci behave almost independently

  • D depends on allele frequencies, so it cannot be compared between studies. D′ and r² are normalised and can.

  • Recombination erodes LD each generation by a factor of (1 − c), so tightly linked loci keep it far longer — that is the basis of association mapping.

  • r² is the statistic for marker selection: an r² of 0.8 means the tag SNP explains 80% of the variance at the causal site.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Entering the haplotype count instead of its frequency.
  • Reading D′ as a correlation — it can be 1 with almost no correlation when one allele is rare.
  • Ignoring population structure, which creates LD between unlinked loci.

sections.title: Calculators that go with this one
sections.html:
Most real jobs need two or three of these together:

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. Genetics odds ratio. Fixation index (Fst).

faq.q: What is a good r² for a tag SNP?
faq.a: 0.8 or above is the usual threshold for a marker to stand in for the causal variant.
Yes — that means the two alleles are found together less often than chance predicts.

faq.q: Why is D′ high while r² is low?
faq.a: When one allele is rare, D′ saturates while r², which accounts for allele frequency, stays low.

faq.q: What does the Linkage Disequilibrium actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns expected AB if independent, D (coefficient of disequilibrium), D′ (normalised) and r². Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
